4.text: The groups of Reindeer Chukchee are as follows: —

5.text: The Indighirka and Alaseya Group, along the rivers of the same names, — 13 camps, with a popu-

6.text: lation of about 150 souls. This is the most westerly group, and its territory is surrounded by

7.text: districts inhabited by Yakut and Tungus. Some of its reindeer-herds consist of as many as

8.text: 5,000 head, and their owners reguiarly supply the Russian town of Sredne-Kolymsk and other

10.text: The Western Kolyma Group, as the name indicates, on the tundra to the west of the Kolyma

11.text: River, — about 35 camps, with a population of 400 souls. This group, on account of a severe

12.text: epidemic of small-pox, which in 1884 devastated it and caused one-third of the population to

13.text: perish, is rather on the decrease. After the epidemic many large herds, left without guards,

14.text: disintegrated, and joined the herds of wild reindeer; while some of the western camps, who

15.text: formerly lived in this district, recrossed the Kolyma River and re-occupied their former territory.

16.text: The Dry Anui Group, between the Arctic Ocean and the Dry Anui River. This group is the

17.text: largest of all, and its camps extend at intervals of from five to ten miles from the right bank

18.text: of the Kolyma, along the Anui, to the confines of the Chaun tundra. The camps number

19.text: about 100. Their herds are not very large, for the most part consisting of from 300 to 400

20.text: head, which is sufficient to supply two families (i. e., from ten to fifteen persons, the average

21.text: size of a camp) with meat, clothing, and trading-skins. Several herds, however, number 2,000-

22.text: 3,000 animals. Farther to the east the herds of this group are of larger size.

23.text: The Large Anui Group, consisting of hardly 20 camps. Their number has been considerably depleted

24.text: by migration southward to the rivers Oloi and Omolon, where at present the most southerly

25.text: portion of the tribe is living. This is a group of about 45 camps, with a population of 500

26.text: souls. Some of their herds are as large as those of the Indighirka, and supply two Russian

27.text: towns — Sredne-Kolymsk and Gishiginsk — with meat. They have no access to the sea,

28.text: however, and consequently live in the mountains during the summer months, so that there have

29.text: been considerable losses in reindeer among them from time to time.

30.text: The Upper Anadyr Group, which comprises about 30 camps. These also resort to the mountains

31.text: in summer. Of late their herds, too, have been greatly reduced.

32.text: The Chaun Group, — about 50 camps, living on the tundra near Chaun Bay. They are separated

33.text: from the Anui Group by the mountains of the watershed. Their herds, like those of the Eastern

34.text: Anui, number about 400 or 500 head, though more numerous herds also occur. The same may

38.text: The Oˊnmɪlɪn (“the inland one”) Group, living between the north bank of the Anadyr River and

39.text: Holy Cross Bay, — about 60 camps. It varies considerably in the proportion and distribution

40.text: of its herds. Many camps are very poor, and live on fish and seal three seasons out of four,

41.text: while others are well-to-do. This whole group includes a number of Maritime Chukchee from

42.text: the Pacific villages who have turned reindeer-breeders within the last thirty years. Their herds

43.text: have not yet had time to become very large.
